implementation_state: All four gates are met and both named defects are repaired, so this moves off FAILED; It moves to DONE because nothing in the application called the rollback path, and it now is: the migration_rollback command reaches MigrationExecutor::rollback through Desktop, and the Cutover page offers it exactly where the state machine permits. The state machine only admits Failed -> RolledBack, so the panel refuses the button elsewhere rather than working around it -- rollback_with ignores a refused transition and would restore the bytes while the record kept denying it, which is an undo whose own record contradicts it. That refusal is why this node is DONE rather than merely reachable: the surface cannot offer an unrecorded restore. Conflict resolution being disconnected from release was repaired by I3's release_resolved, not here: resolve_conflicts had computed a resolution with no production caller since before either node was touched. The rollback defect was that MigrationResult reported state RolledBack and rolled_back true whether or not a byte went back, with restore failures pushed into warnings, errors hardcoded empty and rolled_back a constant -- so a rollback that restored nothing was indistinguishable from a clean one to every caller. rolled_back now answers whether the pre-migration state was actually put back and is false whenever any restore failed, with restored_files and failed_restores naming which file went which way. The restore failure is injected through SnapshotWriter rather than provoked with read-only permissions, because CI runs Linux, macOS and Windows and read-only semantics differ between them; a gate whose outcome depends on the OS is green until it is not. Restore failures are recorded in errors and not only in warnings, because every caller checks errors.is_empty() and none are obliged to read warnings. THE RESTORE PATH HAS SINCE BEEN AUDITED AGAIN AND ONE MORE DEFECT WAS FOUND, this one inside the earlier repair: rolled_back was computed as failed_restores.is_empty, so a rollback that restored nothing failed nothing and reported true. E-118 covered a failed restore and missed an absent one, and because recover passed None on every call, every interrupted migration reported a successful restore while putting no file back. rolled_back now requires at least one file restored and none failed. THAT IS A PUBLIC-FIELD SEMANTIC CHANGE and it is flagged rather than settled: whether restored-nothing should read as success is a judgement rather than a fact, seven fixtures asserted the old wording and were restated rather than deleted, and the control case of a real snapshot restoring successfully still reports true, so the distinction is pinned in both directions. Recovery also could not actually recover: MigrationStore held its state in memory, so a fresh process read Detected and recover refused the three states it exists for, while the snapshot rollback restores from lived in the same process memory. State and snapshot are now persisted and recover loads the snapshot, so an interrupted migration can be undone after a restart rather than merely remembered.
unblock_condition: Close I2 and I3 contracts and pass conflict-safe restore/rollback tests with explicit failure reporting.
notes: The audit decision was preserved as FAILED and is now superseded: the conditions the audit recorded were repaired, and blocked_by is empty because I2 and I3 no longer name an unresolved gate. The status is DONE because a production caller now exists and can be reached by a person.

Whether a dependency's gates being met is what satisfies an edge, or whether the dependency must additionally be INTEGRATED, is answered by the DAG's own rule rather than by preference: blocked_by is defined as a subset of dependencies naming an active unresolved gate. It keys on gates, so met and verified gates close the contract.

MOVED TO DONE BECAUSE ITS SOLE REMAINING REASON WAS UNREACHABLE, and reachability is what this node has always been about. The restore semantics themselves did not change to earn this: rolled_back already answered whether a byte went back and was already false when one did not, and the flag this record kept calling an unsettled semantic change is settled in the only way that was open -- the panel branches on the field rather than on the state, so a rollback that restored nothing renders as a rollback that restored nothing while the machine says RolledBack. Both facts are shown because each is true and the other does not imply it.

THE HONEST LIMIT: a person has not driven a rollback in the running application. The fixtures cover the semantics, the desktop suite covers the gating and the refusals, and the panel is exercised by the layout harness against a failed record with a snapshot -- but that fixture is a rendering, not a cutover that actually failed and was actually undone.
